title: Observability: Metrics, Tracing, Logging
summary: Observability is the ability to ask **new questions** of a running system without shipping new code, built on three pillars: **structured logs** (`log/slog`), **metrics** (Prometheus `client_golang`), and **distributed traces** (OpenTelemetry). The real power comes from **correlation** — stamping every log line and metric exemplar with the active **trace_id** so you can pivot from an aggregate alert to the exact request that caused it.

subtopics.title: Structured logging with log/slog
subtopics.explanation: slog (Go 1.21+) emits key/value records instead of formatted strings, so logs are machine-parseable. A Handler decides the format (JSON, text); Levels gate verbosity; logger.With(...) returns a child logger that attaches fields to every line; and the *Context methods (InfoContext) let you carry request-scoped attributes.

subtopics.title: Metrics with Prometheus client_golang
subtopics.explanation: Counters only go up (requests, errors); Gauges go up and down (in-flight requests, queue depth); Histograms bucket observations (latency) so you can compute quantiles in the query layer. Labels add dimensions, and promhttp.Handler() exposes everything at /metrics for scraping.

subtopics.title: Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry
subtopics.explanation: A TracerProvider creates Tracers that start Spans. A trace is a tree of spans sharing one trace_id; context.Context carries the active span across function and network boundaries (propagators inject/extract W3C traceparent headers). An Exporter ships spans to a backend (Jaeger, Tempo, OTLP collector); a Sampler decides which traces to keep.

subtopics.title: Correlation: logs <-> traces <-> metrics
subtopics.explanation: Pull the trace_id from the span in context and add it to every log line so a single request's logs are greppable, and attach exemplars to histograms so a slow latency bucket links straight to a trace. This pivot — from a dashboard spike to the offending request — is what turns three separate signals into observability.

subtopics.title: RED, USE, and cardinality discipline
subtopics.explanation: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) instruments request-driven services; USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) instruments resources. Crucially, every distinct label-value combination is a separate time series — putting unbounded values (user IDs, raw URLs) in labels causes a cardinality explosion that can OOM your Prometheus server.
subtopics.example: // BAD label: user_id (millions of series). GOOD: route template /users/:id

foundations.overview: Monitoring answers questions you already knew to ask ('is CPU high?'). Observability lets you ask questions you didn't anticipate ('why are checkout requests from this one region timing out only after a deploy?') by emitting rich, structured signals. Go has become the lingua franca of cloud-native observability — Prometheus, Jaeger, Loki, Grafana Tempo, and the OpenTelemetry collector are all written in Go — and the standard library's log/slog plus the official OpenTelemetry and Prometheus client libraries give you idiomatic, low-overhead instrumentation out of the box.
foundations.formalDefinition: Observability is a property of a system measuring how well its internal state can be inferred from its external outputs. In practice it is realized through three correlated telemetry signals — structured logs (discrete events), metrics (aggregatable numeric time series), and distributed traces (causally-linked spans across services) — typically tied together by a propagated trace context.
foundations.whyItMatters: In a distributed Go backend a single user action fans out across many services; without traces you cannot see the causal path, without metrics you cannot spot aggregate regressions, and without structured logs you cannot inspect a specific failure. Observability is what makes on-call sustainable and incidents debuggable, and it is heavily probed in senior/staff backend interviews.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of investigating a crime across a city. Metrics are the city-wide statistics ('break-ins up 12% this week') that tell you something is wrong. Traces are the GPS breadcrumb trail of one suspect's exact route through every building. Logs are the detailed witness statements at each location. The trace_id is the case number written on every document so all three sources can be joined into one story.
foundations.runtimePerspective: slog records are allocated as []slog.Attr and only formatted when a handler is enabled for that level, so disabled debug logs are nearly free. Prometheus metrics are lock-light atomic counters held in process memory and serialized lazily on scrape. OpenTelemetry spans live in the context.Context value chain (an immutable linked list of key/value pairs); starting a span allocates a span object that the SDK batches and exports on a background goroutine, so the hot path mostly does a context write plus an atomic timestamp.
foundations.realWorldUsage: An HTTP middleware extracts the W3C traceparent header into a context, starts a server span, increments an in-flight gauge, and on completion records request count and latency histograms labelled by route and status, while every handler log line carries the trace_id. Dashboards graph RED metrics; alerts fire on error rate or p99; and an engineer clicks an exemplar to jump from the latency spike straight into the slow trace.
foundations.businessImpact: Faster mean-time-to-resolution directly reduces revenue lost during outages and the engineering hours burned on incidents. Good SLO/SLI instrumentation lets a business make data-driven reliability-vs-feature tradeoffs instead of guessing.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Standardized, structured telemetry removes the 'works on my machine / no idea what prod is doing' gap, lets teams share dashboards and runbooks, and makes deploys safe via canary metrics. Poor instrumentation (string-concatenated logs, high-cardinality labels) creates its own outages.
foundations.performanceImpact: Instrumentation is not free: histograms cost memory per bucket per label set, every span has allocation and export overhead, and excessive logging can dominate I/O. The discipline is sampling traces, bounding label cardinality, choosing histogram buckets deliberately, and logging at the right level — keeping overhead in the low single-digit percent.
commonUseCases: RED-method HTTP middleware (request rate, error rate, latency histogram)
Structured request logs correlated by trace_id
Distributed traces across service and database boundaries
USE-method instrumentation of pools, queues, and caches

commonMisconceptions.myth: Logs, metrics, and traces are interchangeable — pick one.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They answer different questions and are most powerful together: metrics tell you something is wrong, traces tell you where, logs tell you why. Correlation by trace_id is the point.

commonMisconceptions.myth: More labels make metrics more useful.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Each unique label-value combination is a separate time series. High-cardinality labels (user IDs, raw URLs, timestamps) cause a cardinality explosion that can OOM Prometheus. Use bounded values like route templates.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must sample 100% of traces to debug effectively.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Head/tail sampling keeps representative or interesting traces (e.g. all errors, all slow requests) at a fraction of the cost; full sampling is usually unaffordable at scale.

commonMisconceptions.myth: slog is just fmt.Sprintf with extra steps.
commonMisconceptions.reality: slog emits structured key/value records that backends can index and query; disabled levels skip formatting entirely, and With() / context attributes propagate fields without restating them on every call.

visualExplorer.title: A request through the three pillars
visualExplorer.caption: Follow one HTTP request as trace context is propagated, a span is created, a metric is incremented, and a structured log line is emitted carrying the trace_id.

config.intro: How an instrumented request produces correlated telemetry, step by step:

steps.name: Extract trace context
steps.detail: Middleware reads the incoming W3C `traceparent` header and uses the OpenTelemetry propagator to build a context.Context that carries the upstream trace_id and parent span id (or starts a fresh trace if none).

steps.name: Start a server span
steps.detail: `ctx, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "GET /orders")` records a child span under the propagated trace. The new ctx now holds the active SpanContext and is threaded into every handler and downstream call.

steps.name: Increment in-flight & count metrics
steps.detail: A Gauge (`http_in_flight`) is incremented on entry and deferred-decremented on exit; on completion a CounterVec (`http_requests_total{route,code}`) is incremented. Labels use the bounded route template, not the raw path.

steps.name: Observe latency into a histogram
steps.detail: The elapsed time is recorded into a HistogramVec (`http_request_duration_seconds`). With exemplars enabled, the observation carries the trace_id so a slow bucket links to the exact trace.

steps.name: Emit a correlated structured log
steps.detail: `log.InfoContext(ctx, "request complete", "route", route, "code", code, "trace_id", traceID)` writes a JSON record. The trace_id ties this log line to the span and the metric exemplar.

steps.name: End span & export
steps.detail: `span.End()` finalizes timing; the SDK batches the span on a background goroutine and an OTLP exporter ships it to a collector. Metrics wait passively in memory until Prometheus scrapes `/metrics`.

interactiveExamples.title: Structured logging with slog: handlers, levels, and With
interactiveExamples.explanation: slog.New wraps a Handler that controls the output format. JSON output is deterministic except for the time field, which we replace via ReplaceAttr so the output is reproducible here. logger.With attaches fields to a child logger so every subsequent line carries them. Note how InfoContext is used to pass a request-scoped context.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: a RED-metrics HTTP middleware
interactiveExamples.explanation: This middleware should measure the three RED signals — request Rate and Errors (via a CounterVec labelled by route and status code) and Duration (via a Histogram). Critically, it must label by the bounded `route` template, never the raw r.URL.Path, to avoid a cardinality explosion. Fill in the deferred observation. Reveal the solution to compare.

checkpoints.prompt: With a JSON handler at LevelInfo (timestamp stripped), what does this print?
options: Nothing — JSON handler needs a level on every call
checkpoints.explanation: The handler's minimum level is Info, so the Debug line is filtered out (and never even formatted). Only the Info record is emitted as JSON. The msg and any key/value pairs become fields; with the timestamp stripped, just level, msg, and port remain.

checkpoints.prompt: You want to compute the p99 latency of an HTTP endpoint in Prometheus. Which metric type should you use?
options: Counter — it only goes up, like total time
Gauge — set it to the latest latency value
Histogram — bucket observations so quantiles are computed at query time
Summary is the only option; histograms cannot produce quantiles
checkpoints.explanation: A Histogram buckets each observation; the histogram_quantile() function then estimates p99 across buckets at query time, and histograms are aggregatable across instances (unlike Summary quantiles). A Counter cannot express a distribution, and a Gauge of 'latest latency' loses the distribution entirely.

checkpoints.prompt: This middleware compiles but melts the Prometheus server in production. What's the bug?
options: WithLabelValues must be called before NewCounterVec
High-cardinality labels: raw URL paths and per-user IDs create unbounded time series (a cardinality explosion)
Inc() must be passed a value to increment by
checkpoints.explanation: Every unique combination of label values is a separate time series stored in memory. raw URL paths (which include IDs, query strings) and user_id produce effectively unbounded series, exhausting Prometheus memory. Use a bounded route template (e.g. "/users/:id") and never put unbounded identifiers in labels — log them or attach to a trace instead.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the line so the structured log carries the active trace's ID for correlation.
checkpoints.codeBefore:
ctx, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "GET /orders")
defer span.End()
traceID := span.SpanContext().TraceID().String()
log.InfoContext(ctx, "request complete",
checkpoints.explanation: slog takes alternating key/value arguments, so you pass the key string "trace_id" followed by its value traceID. This stamps the JSON log record with the same trace_id as the span, letting you grep logs for one request and pivot between logs and traces.

codeLab.title: Build a testable RED-metrics recorder
codeLab.instructions: Implement an in-memory metrics recorder (no Prometheus network, no scraping — fully deterministic) that models the RED method. `NewRecorder()` returns a *Recorder. `Observe(route string, code int, dur time.Duration)` must: (1) increment a per-(route,code) request counter, (2) increment a per-route error counter when code >= 500, and (3) accumulate total duration per route. Provide getters `Count(route string, code int) int`, `Errors(route string) int`, and `TotalDuration(route string) time.Duration`. Make it safe for concurrent use with a sync.Mutex.
hints: Use a struct key {route string; code int} for the counts map so each (route, code) pair is one bounded series.
Only increment the error counter when code >= 500 — 4xx are client errors, not service errors in the RED model.
Guard every map read and write with the same sync.Mutex; run `go test -race` to confirm the concurrent test is clean.

debuggingLab.title: Child spans show up as separate, broken traces
debuggingLab.symptom: In the tracing backend, the database span appears as its own root trace with no parent, instead of nesting under the HTTP request span. Logs also show a different trace_id from the parent.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: OpenTelemetry propagates the active span through context.Context. tracer.Start returns a NEW ctx that contains the just-created span; you must thread THAT ctx into downstream calls. The bug passes r.Context() (the original, which still holds only the server/root span or nothing) to queryDB, so the db.query span can't find the 'handler' span as its parent and starts a fresh trace with a different trace_id.
commonMistakes: Ignoring the ctx returned by tracer.Start and reusing the original context.
Storing a span in a struct field and reading ctx elsewhere instead of passing ctx explicitly.
Starting a goroutine with context.Background() instead of the request ctx, severing the trace.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Thread the context returned by tracer.Start (the one carrying the new span) into queryDB so the db.query span nests correctly.

theory.question: What are the three pillars of observability, and why isn't any one of them sufficient on its own?
theory.directAnswer: Logs (discrete, high-detail events), metrics (cheap, aggregatable numeric time series), and traces (causally-linked spans across services). Each answers a different question: metrics tell you THAT something is wrong and let you alert cheaply; traces tell you WHERE in a distributed call graph the latency or error originates; logs tell you WHY at a specific point. You need all three, correlated by a propagated trace_id, because metrics lack per-request detail, logs don't aggregate or show causality across services, and traces are usually sampled so they're not a complete record.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A model dividing telemetry into three complementary signal types, unified by trace context.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Distributed systems fan a single request across many services; no single signal can be both cheap-to-aggregate and detailed-per-request, so the signals are specialized and correlated.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Metrics are scraped/aggregated (Prometheus), traces are sampled and exported (OpenTelemetry), logs are streamed and indexed (slog -> Loki/ELK); the trace_id stamped on logs and metric exemplars lets you pivot between them.

theory.whyImportant: It frames every senior observability discussion; interviewers want to hear that you reach for the right signal and correlate them rather than over-relying on logs.
theory.realWorldExample: An alert fires on a p99 latency metric; you click the histogram exemplar to open the slow trace, see the db.query span dominates, then read that span's correlated logs to find a missing index.

followUps.question: Where does profiling fit?
followUps.answer: Continuous profiling (e.g. pprof / Pyroscope) is sometimes called a fourth pillar; it explains CPU/memory cost inside a process, complementing traces that span processes.

followUps.question: What is an exemplar?
followUps.answer: A sample observation attached to a histogram bucket that carries a trace_id, letting you jump from an aggregate metric directly to a representative trace.

theory.question: Explain the RED and USE methods. When do you apply each, and how do they map to Prometheus metric types?
theory.directAnswer: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) instruments request-driven services: a Counter for request rate, a Counter for errors, and a Histogram for duration — usually labelled by route. USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) instruments resources like CPU, pools, queues, and caches: a Gauge for utilization (e.g. % busy), a Gauge for saturation (e.g. queue depth / wait count), and a Counter for errors. Use RED for the request path of your service; use USE for the finite resources that service depends on.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two complementary instrumentation checklists popularized by Tom Wilkie (RED) and Brendan Gregg (USE).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: They give a minimal, consistent set of signals so any service or resource can be dashboarded and alerted the same way, reducing guesswork.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: RED's three signals become a CounterVec (requests, with a code label that also yields error rate) plus a HistogramVec (duration). USE's signals become Gauges (utilization, saturation) plus a Counter (errors).

theory.whyImportant: It shows you can design a coherent dashboard/alert strategy rather than emitting ad-hoc metrics, a common staff-level expectation.
theory.realWorldExample: An API uses RED (http_requests_total, http_request_duration_seconds) while its database connection pool uses USE (db_pool_in_use gauge for saturation, db_pool_max for utilization context, db_errors_total counter).

followUps.question: How do you derive error RATE from a Counter?
followUps.answer: In PromQL: rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m]) — rate() turns the monotonic counter into per-second increase.

followUps.question: Why a Histogram and not a Summary for duration?
followUps.answer: Histogram buckets are aggregatable across instances and let you compute quantiles server-side; Summary quantiles are computed per-instance and can't be meaningfully averaged.

scenario.question: Your Prometheus server's memory has tripled over a week and it now OOMs during scrapes, shortly after a team shipped 'richer' HTTP metrics. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: This is a cardinality explosion. Each unique label-value combination is a distinct time series held in memory; the new metrics almost certainly added a high-cardinality label (raw URL path, user ID, request ID, or timestamp). Diagnose with `topk(20, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))` and `count(count by (label)(metric))` to find the offending label, or use the TSDB status page's top series. Fix by replacing unbounded label values with bounded ones — use the route TEMPLATE (/users/:id) instead of the path, drop user_id from labels (log it or attach it to a trace instead), and add relabel/metric_relabel_configs to drop the bad series. Backfill protection: set a series limit per target.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Unbounded growth in the number of metric time series due to high-cardinality labels.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Prometheus stores every distinct label set as its own series in memory; cardinality multiplies across labels, so one unbounded label dominates.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The label set is the series identity; rate(...) and quantiles are cheap, but holding millions of series for the in-memory head block exhausts RAM.

scenario.whyImportant: Cardinality is the most common self-inflicted observability outage and a frequent senior interview scenario.
scenario.realWorldExample: A team labelled a counter with the full request URL including query params; bot traffic generated millions of unique URLs and the series count exploded overnight.

followUps.question: Where SHOULD unbounded identifiers live?
followUps.answer: On logs (indexed but not aggregated) and on trace/span attributes — both handle high cardinality far better than metric labels.

followUps.question: How can you prevent regressions?
followUps.answer: CI checks on metric names/labels, a per-target series limit, and metric_relabel_configs to drop known-bad labels at scrape time.

coding.question: Write a slog.Handler wrapper that automatically injects the trace_id from the context into every log record. Implement `type TraceHandler struct{ slog.Handler }` with a Handle method.
coding.thoughtProcess: slog.Handler has four methods (Enabled, Handle, WithAttrs, WithGroup). Embedding slog.Handler gives us the other three for free; we only override Handle. In Handle we pull the SpanContext from the context, and if it's valid we add a trace_id attribute to the record before delegating to the wrapped handler. Using the context value (not a closure) means the field is always correct for the current request.
coding.lineByLine: TraceHandler embeds slog.Handler, so it satisfies the interface and only overrides Handle. In Handle, trace.SpanContextFromContext(ctx) extracts the active span context; sc.IsValid() guards against requests with no trace. r.AddAttrs appends a trace_id string attribute to the record. We then call the embedded handler's Handle to do the real formatting/writing. NewTraceLogger wires it up around any inner handler (JSON, text), so callers just use *Context log methods and get correlation for free.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) per log call — a context lookup plus one attribute append.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) extra — one attribute per record.

followUps.question: Why override Handle and not Info/Warn?
followUps.answer: slog.Logger's level methods are concrete and ultimately call Handler.Handle; the Handler interface is the only extension point, so wrapping Handle covers all levels.

followUps.question: Why pass context to the log call at all?
followUps.answer: Only the *Context methods (InfoContext, etc.) forward the ctx to Handle; the plain Info methods pass context.Background(), so the handler couldn't find the span.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Centralize instrumentation in middleware and shared libraries, not scattered call sites: one HTTP middleware for RED metrics + tracing + log correlation, one DB/HTTP-client wrapper for downstream spans. Standardize on OpenTelemetry's API so the SDK/exporter is swappable (OTLP to a collector that fans out to Tempo/Jaeger and Prometheus). Treat telemetry conventions (metric names, label sets, log keys) as a versioned contract.
productionDeepDive.performance: Sample traces (head sampling for volume, tail sampling to always keep errors/slow requests) to bound export cost. Choose histogram buckets to match your SLOs rather than defaults, and bound label cardinality aggressively. Gate debug logs behind level checks so disabled logs cost nothing, and batch span export on a background goroutine to keep the request path fast.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Prometheus client metrics are safe for concurrent use; your own recorders must guard shared maps with a mutex or use atomics. context.Context is immutable and goroutine-safe, but when you fan out work into goroutines you must pass the request ctx (and often start a child span per goroutine) so the trace isn't severed and isn't ended early by the parent's span.End().
productionDeepDive.reliability: Telemetry must fail open: a dead trace collector or a slow log sink must never block or crash the request path. Use bounded buffers/queues with drop-on-full semantics for exporters, set export timeouts, and ensure a panic in instrumentation can't take down the handler. Emit a self-metric for dropped spans/logs so you know when you're flying blind.
productionDeepDive.observability: Instrument the instrumentation: export dropped-span counters, exporter latency, and series counts; alert on cardinality growth. Define SLOs as error-budget burn-rate alerts (multi-window, multi-burn-rate) rather than raw thresholds to cut alert fatigue. Make trace_id visible in every log line and in user-facing error responses so support can correlate.
productionDeepDive.security: Telemetry leaks data: never log secrets, tokens, PII, or full request bodies — redact at the handler/slog ReplaceAttr layer. Be careful that span attributes and high-cardinality logs don't capture sensitive identifiers. Secure the /metrics endpoint and the OTLP collector (auth, network policy) since they expose internal topology and traffic patterns.

caseStudies.problem: Storing and querying traces and metrics at petabyte scale cost-effectively.
caseStudies.solution: Object-storage-backed trace store (Tempo) keyed by trace_id, plus horizontally-scalable Prometheus-compatible metrics (Mimir); exemplars link metrics to traces.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Cheap storage and high scale, but trace lookup is by ID (not full-text), pushing the correlation burden onto consistent trace_id propagation.
caseStudies.lessons: Design for correlation up front: if trace_id isn't reliably propagated and logged, cheap by-ID trace storage is useless.

caseStudies.problem: Debugging latency across thousands of microservices where no single team owns the full request path.
caseStudies.solution: Pervasive distributed tracing with context propagation and adaptive sampling, later donated as Jaeger and aligned with OpenTelemetry.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Full visibility into causal paths, but sampling means not every request is captured and propagation must be enforced org-wide.
caseStudies.lessons: Tracing's value is proportional to propagation coverage; one un-instrumented hop breaks the trace, so context threading is a discipline, not a feature.

keyTakeaways: Observability rests on three correlated pillars — structured logs (log/slog), metrics (Prometheus client_golang), and distributed traces (OpenTelemetry) — joined by a propagated trace_id.
Pick the right metric type: Counters for monotonic counts, Gauges for up/down values, Histograms for latency distributions and quantiles; instrument request paths with RED and resources with USE.
Guard cardinality ruthlessly — every label-value combo is a time series; keep unbounded identifiers (user IDs, raw URLs) out of labels and put them in logs or trace attributes instead.

Tracing's payoff depends on threading the context returned by tracer.Start through every call (including goroutines) and stamping trace_id on logs, so you can pivot from a metric spike to the exact request.
